options.text: Respiration that only occurs in plants

questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen. It releases less energy than aerobic respiration because the glucose is only partially broken down.

questions.stem: What is the product of anaerobic respiration in human muscles?
questions.explanation: In animal cells (including human muscles), anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid. The equation is: glucose -> lactic acid.

questions.stem: What is produced during anaerobic respiration in yeast?
questions.explanation: In yeast (and some plant cells), anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide. This process is called fermentation and is used in brewing and baking.

questions.stem: Why does anaerobic respiration release less energy than aerobic respiration?

options.text: The glucose molecule is only partially broken down, so energy remains locked in the products

questions.explanation: In anaerobic respiration, glucose is not fully broken down. The products (lactic acid or ethanol) still contain chemical energy, so less energy is released per glucose molecule.

questions.stem: When do muscles use anaerobic respiration?

options.text: During intense exercise when oxygen cannot be supplied fast enough

questions.explanation: During vigorous exercise, muscles need energy faster than oxygen can be delivered. They switch to anaerobic respiration to continue producing ATP, even though it is less efficient.

options.text: Anaerobic respiration in yeast, producing ethanol and CO2

questions.explanation: Fermentation is anaerobic respiration in yeast and some bacteria. In yeast, glucose is broken down to ethanol and carbon dioxide. This process is used commercially in brewing beer and baking bread.

questions.stem: Why does bread rise when baked with yeast?

options.text: Carbon dioxide gas produced by anaerobic respiration in yeast creates bubbles that expand in the dough

questions.explanation: Yeast in bread dough carries out anaerobic respiration (fermentation), producing carbon dioxide gas. The gas bubbles get trapped in the dough, causing it to rise. The ethanol evaporates during baking.
